title: Administrative Divisions of Afghanistan: Provinces and Districts
source: Common Operational Dataset - Administrative Boundaries (COD-AB), Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), distributed via UN OCHA / Humanitarian Data Exchange
text: Afghanistan's administrative structure consists of 34 provinces (wilayat), which form the first-level administrative division of the country, and 401 districts (woleswali), which form the second-level division beneath the provinces. Provincial administrative boundaries are delineated by the Afghanistan Geodesy and Cartography Head Office (AGCHO), which is recognized as the country's authoritative source for administrative boundary delimitation. The AGCHO boundary dataset is distributed internationally through the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) as part of the Common Operational Datasets (COD) used by the humanitarian community. The current 34-province, 401-district structure was established in the boundary dataset released on 22 October 2019 and was most recently reviewed for accuracy in July 2024, with reviewers determining that no update to the boundaries was required at that time. Each province is subdivided into a number of districts, ranging from as few as 6 districts (Nimroz) to as many as 28 districts (Badakhshan) in the AGCHO dataset. Provinces are governed by a provincial governor, and districts are the primary unit for local public-service delivery, including health, education and security administration.
notes: 34 provinces / 401 districts confirmed consistent across the HDX 'cod-ab-afg' dataset description and UNOSAT GIS metadata for the same AGCHO dataset (afg_admbnda_adm1/2_agcho_20211117).

title: Kabul: National Capital and Capital of Kabul Province
source: General geographic reference, cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Kabul is the national capital of Afghanistan and simultaneously serves as the capital of Kabul Province, one of Afghanistan's 34 provinces. Kabul Province is located in the eastern-central part of the country and borders Parwan, Kapisa, Laghman, Nangarhar, Logar and Maidan Wardak provinces. As the seat of the national government, Kabul city hosts the country's central government ministries and foreign diplomatic missions, and it is the largest urban center among all Afghan provinces. The dual role of Kabul as both national capital and provincial capital is consistent across administrative-boundary datasets maintained by AGCHO and distributed through UN OCHA's Common Operational Datasets programme.
notes: Capital-city designation is well-established, stable geographic fact; marked 'medium' rather than 'high' because it is corroborated across multiple general references rather than drawn from a single named statistical indicator, unlike the World-Bank-sourced documents below.

title: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT)
source: Ministry of Communications and Information Technology, official website
text: The Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) is the government body responsible for telecommunications policy, internet-sector regulation and information-technology development in Afghanistan. Its published areas of responsibility include research, innovation and collaboration in the communications and IT sectors, and it publishes its general plan, policies, laws and regulations on its official website. MCIT is headquartered in Kabul. In late 2021, following the change of government, state telecommunications bodies including the Afghanistan Telecom Regulatory Authority (ATRA), the state-owned operator Afghan Telecom (Aftel), and Afghan Post were brought under the administrative umbrella of MCIT, with ATRA continuing to operate as a non-budgetary regulatory unit under the ministry's oversight. MCIT also lists online public services on its website, including a passport-tracking service and the e-Tazkera (electronic national ID) system.
notes: Ministerial leadership changes frequently and is politically contested (Wikipedia lists conflicting incumbents as of 2026); this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister so the ground truth for questions built on it stays stable. The ATRA/Aftel/Afghan Post restructuring detail is corroborated by an independent telecoms trade-press report (developingtelecoms.com).

title: Afghanistan Gross Domestic Product (GDP), 2023
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators data, Afghanistan's Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at current prices was approximately US$17.15 billion in 2023, up from approximately US$14.50 billion in 2022. GDP is measured as the sum of gross value added by all resident producers in the economy, plus product taxes and minus subsidies, without deductions for depreciation of assets. Dollar figures are converted from Afghanistan's domestic currency (the Afghani) using official exchange rates for the corresponding year. The services sector is the largest contributor to Afghanistan's GDP, followed by agriculture. World Bank data put GDP per capita for the same year at approximately US$378.
notes: Cross-checked against the World Bank series as mirrored by Trading Economics and FRED (Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis), both of which cite the World Bank as the original source.

title: Afghanistan Total Population, 2024
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators
text: World Bank World Development Indicators estimate Afghanistan's total population at approximately 42,647,492 people in 2024, up from approximately 41,454,761 in 2023. The estimate uses a de facto definition of population, counting all residents regardless of legal status or citizenship, with the exception of refugees not permanently settled in Afghanistan. Afghanistan's annual population growth rate was estimated at approximately 2.8% in 2024. The population has a notably young age structure: World Bank data indicate that people aged 0-14 made up approximately 42.9% of the total population in 2024.
notes: Verified directly against World Bank WDI series SP.POP.TOTL and SP.POP.GROW as mirrored on FRED (series POPTOTAFA647NWDB and SPPOPGROWAFG).

title: Internet Usage in Afghanistan, 2023
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators (sourced from the International Telecommunication Union)
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, which source their internet-usage figures from the International Telecommunication Union (ITU), approximately 17.7% of Afghanistan's population were internet users in 2023, up from approximately 17.2% in 2022. 'Internet users' is defined as individuals who used the internet from any location, including via a computer or mobile phone, within the last three months. Internet penetration in Afghanistan has grown slowly and unevenly since 2001, rising from close to 0% in the early 2000s to the current level, and remains among the lowest of any country tracked by the World Bank.
notes: Cross-checked against the World-Bank-sourced series ITNETUSERP2AFG on FRED. An independent estimate from DataReportal's 'Digital 2023: Afghanistan' report puts penetration at 18.4% using a different methodology; the two figures are reported here as distinct series rather than reconciled into one number.

title: Adult Literacy Rate in Afghanistan, 2021
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators
text: The most recent adult literacy rate published by the World Bank for Afghanistan is 37.27% for people aged 15 and above, recorded for 2021. This is up from 33.75% in 2015 and 31.45% in 2011. No more recent World-Bank-published adult literacy estimate for Afghanistan was available at the time of last verification. Adult literacy is defined by the World Bank as the percentage of people aged 15 and above who can, with understanding, read and write a short, simple statement about their everyday life.
notes: 2021 is the latest available data point in World Bank WDI series SE.ADT.LITR.ZS for Afghanistan as of last verification. Researchers citing this record should note the data-year gap explicitly and should not assume the rate has stayed flat since 2021.

title: Afghanistan's Location, Borders, and Topography
source: CIA World Factbook (archived 2023 edition)
text: Afghanistan is a landlocked country in south-central Asia with a total land boundary of approximately 5,987 km. It shares borders with six countries: Pakistan (2,670 km), Tajikistan (1,357 km), Turkmenistan (804 km), Iran (921 km), Uzbekistan (144 km), and China (91 km, via the narrow Wakhan Corridor in the country's far northeast). Afghanistan has no coastline and no maritime claims. The terrain is dominated by rugged mountains, including the Hindu Kush range, with plains in the north and southwest. The country's highest point is Noshak, at 7,492 metres above sea level, and its lowest point is along the Amu Darya river, at 258 metres above sea level.
notes: Border lengths and elevation figures are consistent across the CIA World Factbook's 2023 archived country page; these are official reference figures rather than a single ministry statistic, so cross-checking a second Factbook-style reference before treating a specific km figure as load-bearing for a high-stakes claim is still advisable.

title: Founding of Modern Afghanistan
source: CIA World Factbook (archived 2023 edition)
text: The modern state of Afghanistan traces its founding to 1747, when Ahmad Shah Durrani unified the Pashtun tribes and established the Durrani Empire, initially with its capital at Kandahar; the capital was later moved to Kabul in 1776. Afghanistan served as a buffer state between the British and Russian empires through the 19th century, a period often referred to as 'The Great Game.' It won full independence over its foreign affairs from British control in 1919, following the Third Anglo-Afghan War.
notes: The 1747 founding date and Ahmad Shah Durrani's role are corroborated consistently across the CIA World Factbook, general historical references, and academic sources; treated here as a stable, low-controversy historical fact.

title: Herat, Kandahar, and Mazar-i-Sharif: Major Provincial Capitals
source: General geographic reference, cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Herat is the capital of Herat Province in western Afghanistan, situated in the valley of the Hari River near the borders with Iran and Turkmenistan; it is one of the country's oldest cities and a historic center on the Silk Road. Kandahar is the capital of Kandahar Province in southern Afghanistan and served as the first capital of the Durrani Empire before the seat of government moved to Kabul in 1776. Mazar-i-Sharif is the capital of Balkh Province in northern Afghanistan, close to the borders with Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, and is home to the Shrine of Ali (the 'Blue Mosque'), one of the country's most-visited religious sites.
notes: Population figures for these cities vary substantially across sources (estimates for Herat alone range from roughly 400,000 to over 1.2 million depending on the source and year), because Afghanistan's last full census was in 1979. This document deliberately excludes city population numbers and reports only province-capital pairings and stable descriptive facts; any city population figure encountered elsewhere should be treated as unverified until a specific dated source is checked.

title: Da Afghanistan Bank (Central Bank of Afghanistan)
source: Da Afghanistan Bank, official website; Wikipedia (cross-check)
text: Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB) is the central bank of Afghanistan, established in 1939 and wholly state-owned. It is responsible for formulating and implementing monetary policy, regulating and supervising financial institutions, managing currency issuance, and overseeing the national payment system. DAB is headquartered in Kabul. According to DAB's own published licensing information, Afghanistan's banking sector consists of 12 operational banks: 3 state-owned commercial banks, 7 private banks, and 2 branches of foreign banks. Individual customers are permitted to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (approximately US$5,000) per week from their accounts.
notes: Bank count (12) and withdrawal-limit figures are drawn directly from DAB's own website (dab.gov.af); the 1939 establishment date is corroborated by an independent general reference (Wikipedia) but should ideally be reconfirmed against a DAB annual report if used as a high-stakes Ground Truth answer.

title: Ministry of Public Health (MoPH)
source: Ministry of Public Health, official website
text: The Ministry of Public Health (MoPH) is the Afghan government body tasked with delivering and promoting sustainable, accessible health care services nationwide. Its published mandate covers health-service delivery, health-system policy and planning, and administration and finance for the health sector. MoPH is organized into directorates for policy and planning and for health-service provision, alongside programs such as a national cancer-control program and hospital-reform initiatives. MoPH publishes news, laws, regulations, strategies, and reports on its official website.
notes: As with the telecom ministry record (DOC-003), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since ministerial appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources; the mandate and directorate structure described here are stable regardless of who currently holds the post.

title: Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE)
source: Ministry of Higher Education, official website; academic secondary source (cross-check for founding date)
text: The Ministry of Higher Education (MoHE) is the Afghan government body responsible for regulating, expanding, and developing the country's institutions of higher education. Its responsibilities include developing a national higher-education curriculum, teacher training, in-service training for university faculty, partnerships with international universities, and providing training in accounting, management, and computer literacy for university administration. A separate Ministry of Higher Education was first proposed in 1973 and was formally established in 1977, standardizing what had previously been managed through the Ministry of Education.
notes: The 1977 establishment date is drawn from an academic source discussing the history of Afghan higher-education administration; MoHE's own official website was reachable but did not surface a clearly dated 'about us' history page during verification, so this date is marked verified against a secondary academic source rather than the ministry's own primary documentation.

title: The Afghan Afghani (AFN)
source: Da Afghanistan Bank, official website
text: Afghanistan's official currency is the Afghani, with the ISO 4217 currency code AFN. The Afghani is issued exclusively by Da Afghanistan Bank (DAB), the country's central bank, which is also responsible for printing Afghani banknotes as part of its function as the state's currency-issuing authority. DAB regulations permit individual bank customers to withdraw up to 350,000 Afghanis (roughly US$5,000) per week, or up to 1,000,000 Afghanis per month, from their bank accounts.
notes: Currency code and issuance authority are standard, stable facts; withdrawal-limit figures are current DAB policy as reported and may change without a formal public announcement — treat the specific Afghani amounts as subject to revision.

title: Afghanistan's Merchandise Trade, 2023
source: UNCTADstat (United Nations Conference on Trade and Development)
text: According to UNCTADstat, Afghanistan's merchandise exports were estimated at approximately US$881 million in 2023, while merchandise imports were estimated at approximately US$6.01 billion, producing a merchandise trade deficit of approximately US$5.13 billion for the year. Merchandise export growth was estimated at approximately +7.6% relative to the prior year. Afghanistan's trade balance has been negative for an extended period, reflecting the country's reliance on imported goods relative to its export base, which is concentrated in agricultural products such as dried fruits and nuts.
notes: UNCTADstat labels the 2023 trade figures as estimates ('(e)') rather than final reconciled statistics; treat the exact dollar amounts as approximate rather than precise.

title: Mobile Cellular Connectivity in Afghanistan, Early 2023
source: DataReportal, 'Digital 2023: Afghanistan' report
text: According to DataReportal's 'Digital 2023: Afghanistan' report, there were approximately 26.95 million active cellular mobile connections in Afghanistan at the start of 2023, equivalent to approximately 64.7% of the country's total population at that time. This is distinct from the separate 'internet users' metric reported elsewhere in this Knowledge Base, since a mobile connection does not necessarily include an active data/internet subscription.
notes: DataReportal aggregates data from telecom operators, GSMA Intelligence, and national regulators; it is a widely used industry reference but is not a primary government statistical source, hence 'medium' rather than 'high' trust_level, consistent with the internet-usage document (DOC-006), which flags the same DataReportal report.

title: Life Expectancy at Birth in Afghanistan, 2023
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, life expectancy at birth in Afghanistan was approximately 66.0 years in 2023, up from approximately 65.6 years in 2022. This reflects a substantial long-term increase from approximately 55.0 years in 2000, though Afghanistan's life expectancy remains below the regional and global average.
notes: Cross-checked against the World-Bank-sourced life-expectancy series as mirrored on statisticsoftheworld.com; the exact figure fluctuates slightly (65.98-66.04) across different snapshots of the same underlying World Bank series depending on revision date, so treat 66.0 years as a rounded, not exact, figure.

title: Urban Population Share in Afghanistan, 2024
source: World Bank, World Development Indicators
text: According to World Bank World Development Indicators, approximately 25.7% of Afghanistan's population lived in urban areas in 2024, up slightly from approximately 25.5% in 2023. Afghanistan remains one of the least-urbanized countries tracked by the World Bank, with the large majority of the population living in rural areas.
notes: A separate estimate from Worldometers/DataReportal-style sources puts urban population closer to 26.5-26.8% for similar years using a different methodology; the World Bank WDI figure (25.7%) is used here as the primary Ground Truth since it is the same indicator family used elsewhere in this KB (population, internet users, life expectancy, literacy).

title: Higher Education Institutions and Enrollment in Afghanistan
source: World Bank (2017 feature article); Pajhwok Afghan News (2023 report)
text: As of a 2017 World Bank feature report, Afghanistan had 36 public universities and institutes of higher education, most established or re-established within the preceding decade under the Higher Education Development Project (HEDP). A later report by Pajhwok Afghan News, published in August 2023, cited the Ministry of Higher Education's deputy minister stating that more than 400,000 students in total were studying across the country's universities, with approximately 180,000 enrolled in public universities specifically. In December 2022, the Taliban administration barred women from attending public and private universities, a policy that remained in effect as of the most recent reporting reviewed for this record; this materially affects how any pre-2022 and post-2022 enrollment figures should be compared.
notes: This record deliberately combines two differently-dated sources (a 2017 World Bank count of institutions and a 2023 Pajhwok enrollment statement) because no single, more recent official count of institutions was found during verification; flagged 'medium' trust_level for that reason. The women's-university-access policy point is included because it is necessary context for correctly interpreting enrollment figures, not as commentary.

title: National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA) and the e-Tazkera System
source: National Statistics and Information Authority, official website; Pajhwok Afghan News
text: The National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA), formerly known as the Central Statistics Office, is the Afghan government agency responsible for collecting and maintaining the country's statistical data. It was established in 1972. Through its Civil Registration and Foreign Nationals Registration Department, NSIA is also responsible for registering Afghan citizens and issuing documents including national ID cards (e-Tazkera), birth certificates, death certificates, and marriage certificates. According to a July 2025 report by Pajhwok Afghan News, NSIA officials stated that more than 16 million electronic ID cards had been distributed countrywide to date, of which approximately 10 million were issued after the change of government in 2021.
notes: The e-Tazkera issuance figures come from statements by NSIA officials as reported by Pajhwok, a working Afghan news agency, rather than from a downloadable NSIA statistical bulletin; treated as verified but attributed to the original reporting rather than to a primary NSIA publication.

title: Northern Afghanistan: Provinces and Capitals
source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Northern Afghanistan includes several provinces bordering Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, and Tajikistan across the Amu Darya. Jowzjan Province's capital is Sheberghan. Faryab Province's capital is Maymana. Samangan Province's capital is Aybak. Sar-e Pol Province's capital is Sar-e Pol city. Baghlan Province's capital is Puli Khumri. Kunduz Province's capital is Kunduz city, a major trade hub near the border crossing into Tajikistan. These six provinces, together with Balkh Province (covered separately in this Knowledge Base), make up the country's northern tier.
notes: Province-capital pairings cross-checked across Wikipedia's 'Category:Provincial capitals in Afghanistan' and WorldAtlas's alphabetical province list, both consistent with the 34-province structure in DOC-001. Deliberately excludes city/province population figures, which vary substantially by source and year (see DOC-010's note on the same issue).

title: North-Eastern Afghanistan: Provinces and Capitals
source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: North-eastern Afghanistan is dominated by the Hindu Kush and Pamir mountain ranges. Badakhshan Province, the country's north-easternmost province, has its capital at Fayzabad and contains the narrow Wakhan Corridor, which extends to Afghanistan's short border with China. Takhar Province's capital is Taloqan. Panjshir Province, one of the smaller and newer provinces (separated from Parwan Province in 2004), has its capital at Bazarak, in the Panjshir Valley. Parwan Province's capital is Charikar. Kapisa Province, the smallest of Afghanistan's 34 provinces by area, has its capital at Mahmud-i-Raqi.
notes: Province-capital pairings cross-checked across Wikipedia's 'Category:Provincial capitals in Afghanistan' and WorldAtlas's alphabetical province list, both consistent with the 34-province structure in DOC-001. Deliberately excludes city/province population figures, which vary substantially by source and year (see DOC-010's note on the same issue).

title: Eastern Afghanistan: Provinces and Capitals
source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Eastern Afghanistan borders Pakistan along the Durand Line and includes some of the country's most mountainous terrain. Nangarhar Province's capital is Jalalabad, the region's largest city and a key trade point on the road to Peshawar, Pakistan. Laghman Province's capital is Mihtarlam. Kunar Province's capital is Asadabad. Nuristan Province, a remote, mountainous province in the northeast of this region, has its capital at Parun.
notes: Province-capital pairings cross-checked across Wikipedia's 'Category:Provincial capitals in Afghanistan' and WorldAtlas's alphabetical province list, both consistent with the 34-province structure in DOC-001. Deliberately excludes city/province population figures, which vary substantially by source and year (see DOC-010's note on the same issue).

title: Southern and South-Eastern Afghanistan: Provinces and Capitals
source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Southern and south-eastern Afghanistan border Pakistan and include some of the country's largest provinces by land area. Helmand Province, the largest Afghan province by area, has its capital at Lashkargah. Zabul Province's capital is Qalat (also called Qalat-i Ghilji). Uruzgan Province's capital is Tarinkot. Khost Province's capital is Khost city. Paktia Province's capital is Gardez. Paktika Province's capital is Sharana. Nimroz Province, in the country's south-west, has its capital at Zaranj, near the border with Iran.
notes: Province-capital pairings cross-checked across Wikipedia's 'Category:Provincial capitals in Afghanistan' and WorldAtlas's alphabetical province list, both consistent with the 34-province structure in DOC-001. Deliberately excludes city/province population figures, which vary substantially by source and year (see DOC-010's note on the same issue).

title: Western Afghanistan: Provinces and Capitals
source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Western Afghanistan borders Iran and Turkmenistan. Farah Province's capital is Farah city. Badghis Province's capital is Qala-i-Naw. Ghor Province, a mountainous central-western province, has its capital at Firuzkoh (also known as Chaghcharan). Herat Province, the largest urban center in this region, is covered separately in this Knowledge Base.
notes: Province-capital pairings cross-checked across Wikipedia's 'Category:Provincial capitals in Afghanistan' and WorldAtlas's alphabetical province list, both consistent with the 34-province structure in DOC-001. Deliberately excludes city/province population figures, which vary substantially by source and year (see DOC-010's note on the same issue).

title: Central Afghanistan and the Central Highlands: Provinces and Capitals
source: General geographic reference (Wikipedia province/capital listings), cross-checked against the AGCHO/OCHA administrative boundary dataset
text: Central Afghanistan includes the provinces immediately surrounding Kabul as well as the Central Highlands. Logar Province's capital is Puli Alam. (Maidan) Wardak Province's capital is Maidan Shar. Ghazni Province's capital is Ghazni city, which lies on the Kabul-Kandahar Highway and has historically been an important trade center. Bamyan Province, in the Central Highlands, has its capital at Bamyan city and is home to the Buddhas of Bamiyan archaeological site. Daykundi Province, separated from Uruzgan Province in 2004, has its capital at Nili.
notes: Province-capital pairings cross-checked across Wikipedia's 'Category:Provincial capitals in Afghanistan' and WorldAtlas's alphabetical province list, both consistent with the 34-province structure in DOC-001. Deliberately excludes city/province population figures, which vary substantially by source and year (see DOC-010's note on the same issue).

title: Band-e Amir National Park
source: WorldAtlas (general geographic reference)
text: In 2009, Afghanistan designated part of the Hindu Kush mountains, known as Band-e Amir, as the country's first national park. Located in Bamyan Province, the park contains six deep-blue lakes separated by natural mineral dams: Band-e Gholaman, Band-e Qambar, Band-e Haibat, Band-e Panir, Band-e Pudina, and Band-e Zulfiqar. The park is one of Afghanistan's most visited natural attractions.
notes: Sourced from a general geographic reference (WorldAtlas); the 2009 national-park designation is corroborated by multiple independent tourism and conservation sources.

title: Major Rivers of Afghanistan
source: WorldAtlas (general geographic reference)
text: Afghanistan is drained by several major rivers. The Amu Darya forms much of the country's northern border with Tajikistan, Uzbekistan, and Turkmenistan and is also the country's lowest point at 258 metres above sea level (see DOC-008). The Helmand River, the country's longest river, flows from the Hindu Kush south-west through Helmand Province toward Iran. The Hari River flows through Herat Province toward Turkmenistan and Iran. The Kabul River flows east from the capital, through Nangarhar Province, into the Indus River in Pakistan.
notes: Sourced from a general geographic reference (WorldAtlas); river courses are stable, uncontested geographic facts.

title: Afghanistan's Land Area and Terrain
source: Academic source (terrain/remote-sensing study); cross-checked against general population/geography references
text: Afghanistan has a total land area of approximately 652,000-652,860 square kilometres, making it roughly the world's 40th-to-41st largest country by area depending on the source and year of comparison used. The country's terrain is approximately 75% mountainous, and nearly half of Afghanistan has an average elevation above 6,650 feet (roughly 2,030 metres). This rugged, landlocked terrain (see DOC-008 for border and elevation details) has historically shaped transportation, agriculture, and settlement patterns across the country.
notes: Country-size ranking varies slightly (40th vs 41st) depending on the reference year and which small countries are included in the comparison; treat the ranking as approximate, not exact.

title: Ministry of Energy and Water
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Energy and Water is the Afghan government body responsible for national energy policy and water-resource management, including hydropower development, irrigation infrastructure, and water-basin management. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1980. It is headquartered in Kabul.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Livestock (MAIL) is responsible for agricultural policy, irrigation systems, and livestock and veterinary services in Afghanistan, an economy in which agriculture remains one of the largest employment sectors. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, MAIL was founded in 1918, making it one of the country's oldest government ministries.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Commerce and Industry (MoCI) is responsible for regulating domestic and international trade, licensing businesses, and supporting industrial development in Afghanistan. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1956.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Justice
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Justice is responsible for drafting and publishing Afghanistan's laws and regulations, managing the Official Gazette, and overseeing the country's prison system (Directorate of Prisons and Detention Centers). According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1919.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Transport and Civil Aviation
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Transport and Civil Aviation regulates road, rail, and air transport in Afghanistan, including oversight of the country's international airports in Kabul, Herat, Kandahar, and Mazar-i-Sharif. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1979.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Public Works
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Public Works is responsible for the construction and maintenance of Afghanistan's national highway network and other major public infrastructure projects. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1933.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs is responsible for labour policy, workers' rights, and social-welfare programs, including support for people with disabilities and vulnerable families. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1990.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Rural Rehabilitation and Development (MRRD) is responsible for rural infrastructure and development programs, including rural roads, water supply, and community development projects historically delivered through the National Solidarity Programme and its successor initiatives. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, MRRD was founded in 1954.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Urban Development and Housing
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Urban Development and Housing (MUDH) is responsible for urban planning, municipal infrastructure, and housing policy in Afghanistan's cities. According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 2018, making it one of the country's newest ministries.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Ministry of Mines and Petroleum
source: Wikipedia, 'Ministry of Mines and Petroleum (Afghanistan)'
text: The Ministry of Mines and Petroleum (MoMP) is the Afghan government body responsible for regulating the exploration and extraction of the country's mineral and petroleum resources, including licensing mining contracts. One of the ministry's most prominent projects is oversight of the Mes Aynak copper mine in Logar Province (see the Economy category for further detail on Mes Aynak and Afghanistan's mineral resources).
notes: Sourced from Wikipedia's article on the ministry, cross-referenced against mining-industry press coverage of MoMP's role in the Mes Aynak project (see DOC-046).

title: Ministry of Economy
source: Wikipedia, 'Government ministries of Afghanistan' (tabulated founding years and official websites); each ministry's own official website
text: The Ministry of Economy is responsible for macroeconomic planning, coordinating development programs, and compiling national economic statistics in cooperation with other government bodies such as the National Statistics and Information Authority (NSIA, see DOC-020). According to Wikipedia's tabulation of Afghan government ministries, it was founded in 1920.
notes: Founding year and official domain are drawn from a Wikipedia tabulation of Afghan government ministries; as with other ministry records in this Knowledge Base (DOC-003, DOC-012, DOC-013), this document deliberately avoids naming an incumbent minister, since appointments change and are reported inconsistently across sources.

title: Mobile Network Operators in Afghanistan
source: Operator Watch Blog industry analysis; Capacity Global country profile
text: As of early 2026, Afghanistan's mobile telecommunications market has five main operators: Afghan Wireless Communication Company (AWCC), Roshan, Etisalat Afghanistan, the state-owned Afghan Telecom (branded 'Salaam'), and ATOMA (the successor to MTN Afghanistan after MTN Group divested its Afghan business in January 2025 to Beirut-based M1 New Ventures). Reliable operator-level market-share data is scarce, but industry estimates place Roshan as the leading operator with roughly 35-45% of subscribers, followed by Etisalat Afghanistan at roughly 25-30%, with AWCC and ATOMA holding smaller shares. According to GSMA Intelligence data cited in this analysis, Afghanistan had approximately 22.4 million cellular mobile connections at the end of 2025.
notes: Operator-level market-share figures are explicitly described by the source as 'indicative rather than precise'; treat exact percentages as approximate. This connection-count figure (22.4 million, end of 2025) differs from the DataReportal figure in DOC-016 (26.95 million, early 2023) because they are different years from different data providers — the two are not directly comparable without adjustment.

title: Afghan Wireless Communication Company (AWCC)
source: Digital Logistics Capacity Assessments (logcluster.org)
text: Afghan Wireless Communication Company (AWCC) was founded in 1998 and is headquartered in Kabul. It was the country's first wireless communications provider. AWCC offers 4G LTE mobile service as well as internet and mobile-payment services, and reports approximately five million subscribers across all 34 of Afghanistan's provinces.
notes: Sourced from the Digital Logistics Capacity Assessments (DLCA), a humanitarian-logistics reference maintained by the Logistics Cluster; subscriber counts in the telecom sector generally come from operator self-reporting rather than independent audit.

title: Roshan (Telecom Development Company Afghanistan)
source: Digital Logistics Capacity Assessments; general telecom industry references
text: Roshan (formally the Telecom Development Company Afghanistan Ltd.) launched service in 2003 and is headquartered in Kabul. It is a joint venture between the Aga Khan Fund for Economic Development (AKFED), Monaco Telecom International, and Telia Company. Roshan introduced 3G service in April 2013, with initial coverage in Kabul, Jalalabad, Kandahar, Mazar-i-Sharif, Herat, and Kunduz. Industry estimates place Roshan as one of Afghanistan's largest mobile operators by subscriber count.
notes: Ownership structure and 2003 launch date are corroborated across multiple independent telecom-industry references.

title: Afghan Telecom and the National Fiber-Optic Backbone
source: Academic study of Afghanistan's telecommunications sector
text: Afghan Telecom (branded 'Salaam' for retail mobile service) is a government-owned telecommunications company established in 2006, tasked with operating government telecommunications networks, including Afghanistan's fiber-optic backbone. Afghan Telecom operates as part of the Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT, see DOC-003). As a state-owned operator with a universal-service mandate, it has historically had a smaller subscriber share than the country's private mobile operators.
notes: Sourced from an academic study of Afghanistan's telecommunications sector; the 2006 establishment date and government-ownership structure are corroborated by industry-analysis sources (see DOC-041).

title: Afghanistan's Total Telecommunications Market Size (2024)
source: Academic study citing Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) data
text: According to data attributed to Afghanistan's Ministry of Communications and Information Technology (MCIT) and cited in an academic study of the sector, the total number of active users across Afghanistan's telecommunications market (combining mobile and internet services) reached 25.3 million in 2024. The same study notes a lack of market competition among network operators as a factor that keeps prices relatively high and reduces incentives to improve service quality.
notes: This figure (25.3 million 'active users' in 2024, combining mobile and internet) is a different metric from both the internet-user percentage in DOC-006 and the cellular-connection counts in DOC-016/DOC-041; the three should not be treated as directly comparable without checking each source's exact definition.

title: Mes Aynak Copper Mine
source: The Diplomat; RFE/RL Radio Azadi; USGS Minerals Yearbook (cross-checked)
text: Mes Aynak, located approximately 40 kilometres south-east of Kabul in Logar Province, is one of the world's largest known copper deposits. Estimates of the deposit's size vary significantly by source: a 2021 industry filing by the Metallurgical Corporation of China (MCC) put contained copper at approximately 11.08 million metric tons, while other press reports cite figures ranging from roughly 5.5 to over 12 million metric tons. In July 2024, representatives of Afghanistan's Taliban government and Chinese engineers held a groundbreaking ceremony for initial infrastructure (an access road) at the site, after a 30-year lease originally signed with MCC in 2008 had been delayed for approximately 16 years due to security and contractual issues.
notes: Reserve-size estimates vary substantially across sources (5.5 to 12+ million metric tons of contained copper) and should be treated as estimates, not a single verified figure; this document deliberately reports the range rather than picking one number. Overall Afghan mineral-resource valuations (frequently cited as '$1-3 trillion') are even less precise and are not treated as Ground Truth-quality figures.

title: Afghanistan's Lithium and Rare Earth Mineral Deposits
source: Geopolitical Monitor; Eurasia Review (cross-checked, USGS-attributed estimates)
text: Afghanistan is reported to hold substantial lithium and rare-earth-element (REE) deposits, identified primarily in Ghazni, Nuristan, Helmand, Kunar, and Badakhshan provinces. Citing U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) estimates, press sources report Afghanistan's rare-earth deposits at approximately 1.4 million metric tons, alongside large iron-ore deposits (the Hajigak deposit; see DOC-048). As of the sources reviewed, these lithium and rare-earth deposits remain largely unexploited, without confirmed large-scale extraction contracts comparable to the Mes Aynak copper project.
notes: Aggregate mineral-value estimates for Afghanistan vary enormously across sources (from roughly $1 trillion to $3 trillion) and are frequently repeated without a clear primary citation; marked 'low' trust_level because these figures function more as widely-repeated estimates than as verified, audited reserve data. Should not be used as a high-confidence Ground Truth figure without further primary-source verification.

title: Hajigak Iron Ore Deposit
source: Geopolitical Monitor; RFE/RL (cross-checked)
text: The Hajigak iron-ore deposit, located west of Kabul, is described in press coverage as one of Afghanistan's largest iron-ore deposits, with estimates of up to approximately 2 billion metric tons of high-grade ore. A Brookings Institution estimate cited by RFE/RL separately put Afghanistan's total iron-ore reserves (not limited to Hajigak) at approximately 2.3 billion metric tons. As with other Afghan mineral deposits, large-scale extraction at Hajigak has historically been limited by security conditions and lack of transport and power infrastructure.
notes: Reserve estimates for Hajigak specifically versus Afghanistan's total iron-ore reserves are reported inconsistently across sources and may be conflated in some press coverage; treat the 2 billion / 2.3 billion figures as approximate and possibly overlapping rather than as two independently confirmed numbers.

title: Mining Contracts and Foreign Investment in Afghanistan Since 2021
source: Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime
text: Since returning to power in 2021, Afghanistan's Taliban administration has sought to expand revenue from the country's mineral sector. According to an analysis by the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, the administration awarded at least 205 mining contracts to more than 150 companies between 2021 and early 2025. In September 2023, new mining deals worth more than US$6.5 billion were announced, and in May 2024 the Taliban-controlled Ministry of Mines and Petroleum (MoMP) stated that it had secured investment commitments worth more than US$7 billion from China, Qatar, Turkey, Iran, and the UK.
notes: Contract and investment-value figures are self-reported by the Ministry of Mines and Petroleum as relayed through secondary press/analysis sources; the underlying contract details are described by the source itself as 'undisclosed', so these totals should be treated as officially claimed figures rather than independently audited ones.

title: Median Age and Fertility Rate in Afghanistan
source: UN Department of Economic and Social Affairs, Population Division (via Worldometer/Our World in Data)
text: According to the UN Population Division's World Population Prospects (2024 revision), Afghanistan's median age is approximately 17.4 years, reflecting a very young population structure. Afghanistan's total fertility rate was approximately 4.84 births per woman in 2023, among the higher fertility rates outside of Africa, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data. This fertility rate has been on a long-term declining trend from higher levels in previous decades, but remains well above the global replacement-level rate of approximately 2.1 births per woman.
notes: Sourced from UN Population Division estimates as aggregated by Our World in Data and Worldometer; these are demographic estimates and projections rather than a direct national census count, since Afghanistan's last full census was conducted in 1979.

title: Population Density and Land Area of Afghanistan
source: Our World in Data; Worldometer (cross-checked, both citing UN Population Division)
text: Afghanistan's population density was approximately 63.8 people per square kilometre in 2023, according to Our World in Data's analysis of UN Population Division data, calculated against the country's total land area of approximately 652,860 square kilometres (see DOC-029). As of 2020 estimates cited by the same source, roughly 15.6% of Afghanistan's population lived in rural areas, 44.7% in towns, and 39.7% in cities under one classification scheme; this differs somewhat from the simpler urban/rural split reported by the World Bank in DOC-018, since different sources use different urban/rural/town classification methodologies.
notes: The rural/town/city breakdown in this document uses a three-category classification that differs from the two-category (urban/rural) World Bank methodology used in DOC-018; the two should not be directly combined or compared without checking each source's exact category definitions.

title: Recent Changes in Girls' Primary School Enrollment
source: UNESCO data as reported by UN News
text: According to UNESCO data reported by UN News, Afghanistan had approximately 5.7 million girls and boys enrolled in primary school in 2022, down from approximately 6.8 million in 2019. UN News attributes this decline in part to the Taliban administration's restrictions on female teachers instructing male students, which has worsened an existing teacher shortage, alongside broader socioeconomic pressures on families. Girls' enrollment in primary education (technically still permitted under the Taliban administration for girls under approximately 12 years old) has fallen since 2021, distinct from the separate restriction on women's access to secondary and university education (see DOC-019).
notes: This factual enrollment decline and its officially reported causes are widely corroborated by UN agencies; presented here as reported statistics and attributed causes rather than as editorial commentary, consistent with how this Knowledge Base handles the related university-access policy noted in DOC-019.

title: Kabul University
source: Kabul Municipality (official government source); Wikipedia (cross-check)
text: Kabul University, Afghanistan's oldest public university, was founded in 1932 (1311 Solar Hijri), according to Kabul Municipality's official website. It began with a single Faculty of Medicine, taught initially by two professors to a class of 16 students. The university operated under the Ministry of Education until 1946, when it became an independent institution overseen by a newly established Ministry of Higher Education (see DOC-013). Kabul University has since expanded to more than 20 faculties, including engineering, agriculture, social sciences, and foreign languages, and its main campus spans more than 100 hectares in Kabul.
notes: Founding year (1932) and early history are drawn directly from Kabul Municipality's official government website, cross-checked against Wikipedia and Encyclopedia Britannica, which broadly agree on the 1931-1932 founding period and 1932 Faculty of Medicine start; some sources describe 1931 as when the university was authorized versus 1932 when it opened.

title: Kabul Polytechnic University
source: Wikipedia, 'Kabul Polytechnic University'
text: Kabul Polytechnic University (KPU) is one of the major public universities in Kabul, Afghanistan. It was established on 13 October 1963 on a campus of approximately 72 hectares to the east of the Bagh-e Bala Palace, originally under the name Kabul Polytechnic Institute. KPU offers 8 faculties and 20 departments, with a particular focus on engineering and technical education, and its campus facilities include classrooms, laboratories, a library, and workshop space.
notes: Sourced from Wikipedia's article on the university; the 1963 establishment date and campus details are internally consistent but were not independently cross-checked against the university's own official website (kpu.edu.af) during this verification pass.

title: Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat (DABS) - National Electricity Utility
source: Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat, official website; Devex organization profile (cross-check)
text: Da Afghanistan Breshna Sherkat (DABS) is Afghanistan's national electricity utility, incorporated on 4 May 2008 (15 Saur 1387) as a limited-liability company wholly owned by the Government of Afghanistan, replacing the former Da Afghanistan Breshna Moassassa. DABS is responsible for electricity generation, import, transmission, and distribution nationwide on a commercial basis. Afghanistan remains substantially dependent on imported electricity from neighboring countries, including Iran, Uzbekistan, Turkmenistan, and Tajikistan, particularly during winter months and periods of peak demand, since domestic generation capacity covers only a fraction of national demand.
notes: Incorporation date and ownership structure are drawn from DABS's own official website and corroborated by an independent organizational profile (Devex); specific generation-capacity figures (e.g. megawatt totals) are reported in current news coverage but change frequently as new projects come online, so this document deliberately reports the structural import-dependency fact rather than a specific, fast-changing capacity number.

title: Afghanistan's UNESCO World Heritage Sites
source: UNESCO World Heritage Centre (official website)
text: Afghanistan ratified the UNESCO World Heritage Convention on 20 March 1979 and has two properties inscribed on the World Heritage List. The first, the Minaret and Archaeological Remains of Jam, was inscribed in 2002; located in Ghor Province beside the Hari River, the 65-metre minaret is built entirely of baked brick and decorated with Kufic and Naskhi calligraphy. The second, the Cultural Landscape and Archaeological Remains of the Bamiyan Valley, was inscribed in 2003; the valley includes the site of the two monumental Buddha statues destroyed by the Taliban in March 2001. Both properties are also listed on UNESCO's List of World Heritage in Danger. Afghanistan additionally has four properties on UNESCO's Tentative List, an inventory of sites the government intends to consider for future nomination.
notes: Inscription years, site counts, and Tentative List status are drawn directly from UNESCO's own official World Heritage Centre website (whc.unesco.org), the primary authoritative source for World Heritage designations.
